title: Would you believe me if I said Titanic is one of my favorite movies, ...
transcript: I rarely see a theatre production twice, and maybe this was a good reminder of why. For those who don't know Titanique, it's a musical parody of the movie Titanic, told through the sort of deranged lens of Celine Dion, who claims to have actually been on the ship herself. And when I saw the show off-Broadway three years ago, I praised it for its clever concept and the clarity of their comedic vision. Like, you could tell it was created by a group of friends who had the same sense of humor. And I still felt a lot of that in the Broadway transfer, especially in the first half, where I did find myself laughing a lot. I also remember thinking three years ago that the second half goes a little off the rails and gets overburdened with musical numbers at the expense of the comedy. But I was very willing to forgive that, whereas this time I actually found it quite exhausting. And I've three potential theories as to why that is. First of all, it might just be that it was my second viewing, that some of the charm and novelty had worn off. Secondly, the show actually did run longer. I don't know if they added stuff, but she literally says in the show that it's 90 minutes long, and the press performance I attended ran almost two hours. And honestly, I really felt the length. But that kind of leads to my third theory, which Is that the general vibe of their Broadway glow-up is a lot more bombastic and maybe a bit overwrought. Part of the clever conceit is that they can get away with a lot of anachronisms and wild tangents because it's told through the lens of such a hilariously unreliable narrator. And where a lot of jukebox musicals struggle to make their songs feel organic in the narrative, here, the incongruous shoehorning of Celine Dion hits into Titanic is very much the joke. It's justified by the concept. But seeing it this time, I felt like they had lost track of that framing a bit. It felt less like the deluded daydreams of a pop star and more like The Cast of Titanique The Broadway Show having fun breaking the fourth wall and putting on the most relentlessly energetic musical extravaganza they could muster. Don't get me wrong, Marla Mindelle’s performance is as delightful as ever and does a lot to anchor the show, so to speak, but a lot of the supporting performances felt more like they were operating as individuals competing for the spotlight and less like a coherent comedic ensemble. One of my favorite performances in this production was actually Melissa Barrera as Rose, because as she was kinda sneaky-funny while letting the parody element speak for itself. Last thing I'll say is that I know some will be tempted to comment that I'm overthinking it, I'm being too critical. It's not that serious. Just Let the show be a fun time, blah, blah, blah. And to those people, I say, as always: first of all, you’ve come to the wrong page. But more importantly, musical comedy is a legitimate art form that is difficult to do well. And if you had fun with the show, that's great. But implying that it's not worth criticizing is more of an insult to these artists than anything I said in this video.
classificationReason: Creator attended the Broadway transfer and shares detailed first-hand critical opinions, comparing it to their off-Broadway viewing three years prior. Notes the second half felt exhausting this time and offers theories as to why.
